newsitem.title: USA: US government considers new theory on Gulf disease.
newsitem.headline: US government considers new theory on Gulf disease.

text.p: Government experts will look into a scientist's theory that bacteria possibly used as a biological weapon may be responsible for some illnesses suffered by Gulf War veterans, a spokesman said on Friday.

Walter Reed Army Medical Centre spokesman Ben Smith said the investigation was in "very preliminary stages." Representatives from the Defence and Veterans Affairs departments, the National Institutes of Health and independent scientists will meet early in the new year to discuss how to proceed.

Biochemist Garth Nicolson of the Institute for Molecular Medicine in Irvine, California, has proposed to the Defence Department that it fund an independent study of his research into mycoplasma, a form of bacteria that can cause disease.
Nicolson has successfully treated with antibiotics some sick veterans who had mycoplasma in their blood and believes the bacteria were genetically altered for use as a biological weapon.

Prompted by Representative Norm Dicks, a Washington state Democrat, a small group of experts met at Walter Reed in Washington this week and agreed to follow up on Nicolson's research, Smith said. Dicks read about the research in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer newspaper.

The Pentagon has been studying the causes of what veterans of the 1991 Gulf War with Iraq call "Gulf War syndrome." There are numerous theories about what causes such symptoms as chronic fatigue, depression, muscle and nerve disorders and other problems for the veterans. Some experts point to exposure to Iraqi stores of chemical weapons while others think medicines provided to the soldiers might be responsible.
